title: Advanced SQL
subtitle: 70% of the AE job. Lift it from "works for this report" to "works in a 100M-row Spark cluster."
desc: Window functions, dedupe, fan-out, NULL traps, query plans.

quiz.q: Most recent row per account_id from CDC?
opts: Dedupes by all cols, not latest.
ROW_NUMBER() PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC = 1
One row total, not per account.

recap: Every dbt model is CTEs top-to-bottom.
Master the seven window functions.
Test grain after every join: count(*) vs count(distinct pk).
NULL traps: =, NOT IN, COUNT(col).
In a CDC pipeline: __is_deleted = false on every kafka_cdc.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1 — CTEs over subqueries
screens:
Every dbt model is a top-down CTE chain. Nested subqueries become unreadable past 2 levels.

-- 🟢 AE style
with active_jobs as (
  select job_id, account_id, created_at
  from {{ ref('stg_jobs') }}
  where __is_deleted = false
),
job_counts as (
  select account_id, count(*) as job_count
  from active_jobs
  group by account_id
)
select * from job_counts where job_count > 5;

Production gotcha
Always filter __is_deleted = false on Kafka CDC tables.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.3 — Fan-out, the silent killer
screens:
100 orders × 5 items per order = 500-row join. SUM(order_value) is now 5× the truth.

-- ❌ wrong
select sum(o.order_value)
from orders o
join order_items i on i.order_id = o.id;

-- ✅ correct: aggregate one side first
with items_per_order as (
  select order_id, count(*) as item_count
  from order_items group by order_id
)
select sum(o.order_value)
from orders o
left join items_per_order i on i.order_id = o.id;

Always test grain after a join
count(*) vs count(distinct pk). Differ → fan-out.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.4 — NULL traps
screens:
• NULL = NULL is NULL. Use IS NULL.
  • NOT IN (subquery) returns ZERO rows if subquery has any NULL. Use NOT EXISTS.
  • COUNT(*) counts NULLs; COUNT(col) ignores them.
  • SUM(NULL + 1) = NULL — wrap in COALESCE.

  • COUNT(*) counts NULLs; COUNT(col) ignores them.
  • SUM(NULL + 1) = NULL — wrap in COALESCE.

bossQuestions.q: You need to keep the most recent record per account_id from a CDC stream where many rows share the same key. What's the right approach?

opts.explain: DISTINCT collapses by all columns — won't give you "most recent" semantics.

opts.text: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1
opts.explain: Correct — ROW_NUMBER partitioned by account_id, ordered by updated_at DESC, filtered to rn=1.
GROUP BY MAX(updated_at) loses the rest of the row's columns.
LIMIT 1 only gives one row total, not one per account.

bossQuestions.q: You join orders (1M rows) to order_items (5M rows). What MUST be true if you then aggregate SUM(orders.value)?

opts.text: The sum will be wrong (inflated by fan-out) unless you aggregate items first.
opts.explain: Right — each order row is duplicated by N items, inflating the sum by N×.

opts.text: The sum will be correct because SQL handles duplicates.
opts.explain: SQL doesn't magically deduplicate values across joined rows.

opts.text: The sum is fine if you GROUP BY order_id.
opts.explain: GROUP BY changes the granularity but doesn't fix the duplicated value column.

opts.text: Adding DISTINCT to the sum fixes it.
opts.explain: DISTINCT doesn't address the fundamental fan-out.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3 — pandas → PySpark, the lazy world
screens:
PySpark is pandas-adjacent but lazy and distributed. Transformations build a plan; only an action (show/collect/write) triggers execution.

# pandas
df.groupby('account_id')['value'].sum()

# PySpark
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
df.groupBy('account_id').agg(F.sum('value'))

# still no execution! actions trigger:
df.show()

lessons.title: Lesson 2.4 — Patterns you'll use
screens:
Idempotent CLI

import click
from datetime import date
@click.command()
@click.option('--run-date', default=lambda: str(date.today()))
@click.option('--full-refresh', is_flag=True)
def main(run_date, full_refresh):
    df = extract(run_date)
    load(transform(df), run_date, full_refresh=full_refresh)

Retries with exp backoff

from tenacity import retry, wait_exponential, stop_after_attempt
@retry(wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, max=30), stop=stop_after_attempt(5))
def fetch(url):
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

bossQuestions.q: In PySpark, you call df.filter(...) then df.groupBy(...). Nothing runs. Why?

opts.explain: PySpark cluster is fine — the operations just haven't triggered yet.

opts.text: Spark is lazy — only an action (show/collect/write) triggers execution.
opts.explain: Right — Spark is lazy. Only an action (show, collect, write) triggers execution. Transformations build a plan.
You don't need explicit caching for execution.

opts.text: filter and groupBy block each other.
opts.explain: Filter and groupBy aren't blocked; they're just deferred.

bossQuestions.q: You're working on a feature branch. Main has new commits you need. What's the safer + cleaner approach?

opts.explain: Force-pushing main would overwrite everyone's work.

title: Data Modeling
subtitle: The highest-leverage skill. This is where AE earns its title.
desc: Star schema, SCDs, grain, dimensional thinking.

quiz.q: Revenue must reflect account tier at time of event. Pattern?
opts: SCD Type 2, joined on date range
Versioned tiers; fact joins to version valid on event date.

recap: Star schema = facts (events) + dims (entities).
Declare grain on every fact. Honor it in every join.
SCD2 for history; Type 1 for current-only.
3-layer dbt: staging → intermediate → marts.
Anti-patterns: one big table, mixing grains.

bossQuestions.q: A stakeholder asks "show me revenue by account, where 'account tier' should reflect the tier they were on at the time of revenue." Which modeling approach do you need?

opts.explain: Type 1 overwrites — you'd lose the historical tier.

opts.text: SCD Type 2 on dim_accounts, joined on a valid date range
opts.explain: Right — SCD Type 2 keeps versioned tier rows with valid_from/valid_to. Fact joins to the dim row valid on the revenue date.

opts.text: A single dim_accounts row per account
opts.explain: A single dim row per account loses history by definition.

opts.text: COALESCE the current tier with a fallback
opts.explain: COALESCE doesn't reconstruct historical state.

title: Data Warehousing
subtitle: Why your query is slow — and how to make it 100× faster at the same cost.
desc: OLAP vs OLTP, columnar, partitions, Delta Lake internals.

quiz.q: 2B-row Delta partitioned by year. Query filters event_date. Cheapest fix?
opts: Add AND year = 2026 to enable partition pruning.

recap: OLAP = columnar + distributed + decoupled.
Parquet base; Delta adds ACID + time travel.
4 levers: partition pruning, predicate pushdown, projection, broadcast.
Don't over-partition; Z-order / Liquid for high-cardinality.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.2 — Columnar storage
screens:
Row store: [id1, name1, age1] [id2, name2, age2] …

Column store: [id1, id2, …] [name1, name2, …] [age1, age2, …]

Implication: SELECT AVG(age) reads ONLY age. SELECT * reads everything.

Why SELECT * is bad in OLAP
10-50× more I/O than needed.

bossQuestions.q: Your dbt model on a 2B-row Delta table runs in 4 minutes. The query filters WHERE event_date >= '2026-05-01' but the table is partitioned by year. What's the cheapest first move?

opts.explain: Bigger cluster masks the problem but burns money.

opts.text: Add AND year = 2026 to use partition pruning, then consider repartitioning by date_day.
opts.explain: Right — the filter only prunes if it touches the partition column. Adding "AND year = 2026" lets partition pruning skip all other years.
Indexes aren't a primary concept in columnar warehouses.
Caching helps repeat queries, not the first run.

bossQuestions.q: Your incremental model added a new column. Running dbt run fails with a column-mismatch error. Cheapest fix?

opts.text: Drop the table manually and re-run.

title: Databricks & Spark
subtitle: The platform you already use — but probably under-use.
desc: Spark UI, joins, skew, Photon, Unity Catalog.

quiz.q: Join 12 min, EXPLAIN shows SortMergeJoin. Dim only 5MB. Fix?
opts: Force broadcast — small dim should never sort-merge.

recap: Driver schedules, executors run, shuffles cost. Photon = free speedup.
Transformations lazy, actions trigger.
Skew = #1 hidden killer — watch straggler tasks.
Broadcast small dims; sort-merge big-vs-big.
Delta: OPTIMIZE + ZORDER (or Liquid); time travel for debugging.

lessons.title: Lesson 7.1 — Spark architecture
screens:
Driver coordinates. Multiple Executors run tasks parallel. Data partitioned across executors. Driver builds DAG of stages.

  • Shuffles = data movement between executors. Expensive.
  • Transformations = lazy (filter, groupBy).
  • Actions = trigger execution.
  • AQE = runtime re-optimisation.
  • Photon = vectorised native engine. Free speedup.

screens:
StrategyDescription
Broadcast Hash JoinSmall to all executors. No shuffle. FASTEST.
Sort-MergeBoth shuffled, sorted, merged. Big-vs-big default.
Shuffle HashBoth shuffled; hash on smaller.
BNLJ (Cartesian)"You broke something" join.

lessons.title: Lesson 7.3 — Skew, the #1 hidden killer
screens:
One key has 90% of rows → one task does 90% of work, others idle.

Diagnose

Spark UI → Stages → ONE task 10× the rest. That's skew.

Three fixes

# 1. AQE (free)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")
# 2. Salt the heavy key
df.withColumn("salt", (F.rand()*10).cast("int"))
# 3. Broadcast small side
F.broadcast(small)

bossQuestions.q: Your join takes 12 minutes. EXPLAIN shows SortMergeJoin. The dim table is only 5 MB. What's the fix?

opts.explain: Bigger cluster does linear improvement — broadcast is exponential.

opts.text: Add /*+ BROADCAST(dim) */ hint or raise autoBroadcastJoinThreshold.
opts.explain: Right — force broadcast with the hint. Or raise spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold if 5 MB falls under your current limit.

opts.text: Add an index on the join key.
opts.explain: Indexes aren't a primary Spark concept.
Caching doesn't change join strategy.

title: Orchestration
subtitle: DAGs, schedules, retries, SLAs — making "run every morning" reliable.

quiz.q: DAG failed mid-run yesterday. Re-trigger → duplicates in output. Root cause?
opts: Retries don't cause dupes if task is idempotent.
Task isn't idempotent — INSERT instead of MERGE.

recap: DAG = tasks + deps. Orchestrator: schedule, retries, alerts, SLAs.
Idempotency non-negotiable: MERGE or delete-then-insert.
Airflow industry default; Dagster the asset-first contender.
Sensors for unpredictable upstream; cron for fixed-time.

lessons.title: Lesson 8.2 — Idempotency (non-negotiable)
screens:
Run twice for same date → same result. Otherwise retries corrupt data.

  • Bad: INSERT INTO fact_x — duplicates on retry
  • Good: MERGE INTO fact_x USING ... ON id = id
  • Better: DELETE WHERE date = '{{ ds }}'; INSERT
  • Best: dbt incremental with unique_key

bossQuestions.q: Your DAG failed mid-run yesterday. You re-trigger it today. The output table has duplicated rows. What's the root cause?

opts.explain: Airflow retries don't cause duplicates if the underlying task is idempotent.

opts.text: Task isn't idempotent — likely uses INSERT, not MERGE/upsert.
opts.explain: Right — pure INSERTs append on every run. Switch to MERGE or delete-then-insert for the affected partition.
Retries doesn't set the count too high — it's the task semantics that matter.
Schedule timing doesn't cause duplication.

lessons.title: Lesson 9.2 — CDC deep dive

CDC reads the DB's transaction log (MySQL binlog, Postgres WAL) and emits one event per row change.

Typical stack

Prod DB → Debezium → Kafka → Spark Streaming → Delta Bronze → dbt → Marts

  "ts_ms": 1716000000000,
  "before": { "id": 1, "status": "active" },
  "after":  { "id": 1, "status": "closed" }
}
